chapter_title: Concerning the Dragon with Fourteen Heads; what it

6.original: [and reveal its likeness and its observation above and below, it wages war by]
6.content: and reveal its likeness and its observation above and below, it wages war by

spiritual_reading:
# Spiritual Translation: The Dragon of the Selfhood

---

**¶2:** There never exists a ruling evil of the selfhood possessing fourteen governing falsities in the merely natural person, as those who teach from external knowledge alone declare. Rather, this is a teaching concerning interior spiritual states.

**¶3:** Again, this is how the natural mind [GAP-1] relates to it, inasmuch as it is understood to be the selfhood ruling through the external person [GAP-2]. I will open this to your understanding [GAP-3]: the ruling evil of the selfhood is this governing principle [GAP-4] of the natural and unregenerate person [GAP-5]. Also the fourteen dominant falsities that are distributed throughout the selfhood are these:

**¶4:** The seven modes of perception seated in the intellectual part of the external person are: the two faculties of understanding by which one apprehends truth intellectually; the two faculties of obedience by which one receives truth; the two faculties of discerning spiritual quality by which one perceives the nature of what flows in; also the faculty of discriminating appetite [GAP-6] by which one selects, receiving there the various qualities of good and truth — and their opposites — that present themselves in every form.

**¶5:** These are the seven governing falsities of the selfhood that rule through the seven perceptive faculties belonging to the interior rational part of the person; [GAP-7] and those belonging to the lower, exterior natural part. The seven falsities ruling through the volitional and appetitive nature are these: the two [GAP-8]; the two [GAP-9] dominant powers [GAP-10] corresponding to the seven governing falsities that operate from above in the understanding; so together with those operating below in the will, they complete and constitute fourteen dominant falsities of the selfhood.

**¶6:** Conversely, the five hidden seats of evil about which the ancients taught, where the selfhood is concentrated and from which it exerts its force, are these: the first is the faculty of outward expression and communication; the second is the thought-life through which spiritual respiration occurs; the third is the will itself; the fourth is the bitter and vindictive affection that corrupts purification; the fifth is the vital force of truth dwelling among them, now perverted and falsified. Again, if the selfhood shall project outward from these hidden seats [GAP-11: REVIEW and manifest its character and its vigilance over both the rational and the natural faculties, it wages spiritual combat by means of] its fourteen governing falsities.

**¶7:** Whoever comes to recognize these falsities together with the selfhood — which is the governing thought-life of the unregenerate natural person — and enters into spiritual combat against it and prevails and puts it to death within himself [GAP-12: — that person is called a regenerate being.]

**¶8:** So, behold, I have laid open to you the nature of the selfhood that rules with its fourteen dominant falsities and five hidden seats of evil, within which it lies concealed and undetected. It operates through them according to [GAP-13: its ruling love and its insatiable appe]tite at every moment.

reconstructions.reconstructed_text: There is never a Dragon in the flesh with fourteen heads, as the Magi say! Rather, this is a spiritual lesson.

Again, this is how this earth [is likened] to it, as it is accounted a corporeal Dragon [in the body] I will instruct you [about this] the Dragon is this doctrine [and thought] of the flesh [and of the body] also the fourteen heads that are distributed over the Dragon are these.

The seven sense organs on the head of the body are the two of sight by which one sees; the two of sound by which one hears; the two of scent by which one smells; also the tongue [of taste] by which one selects, receiving there the different tastes that occur in every form.

These are the seven heads of the Dragon, the seven sense organs that are on the upper part of the person; [and also seven are] below. The seven of the torso are these: two [of the hands]; the two [of the feet] ruler [over against] the seven heads that are above; so with the ones below they total and make fourteen heads of the Dragon.

Conversely, the five dens about which they have spoken, where the Dragon is congregated and protrudes, are these: the first is the tongue; the second is the lungs; the third is the heart; the fourth is the spleen; the fifth is the blood that dwells in them. Again, if it shall look out from them [and reveal its likeness and its observation above and below, it wages war by] its fourteen heads.
Whoever will recognise them with the Dragon, which is the thought of the body, and struggles with it and is victorious and kills it in them [that one, he is called a slayer of the Dragon]

So, behold, I have taught you of the Dragon that exists with its fourteen heads and five dens, wherein it is concealed and hidden. It does through them [all that it wills, pursuing its lust and its des]ire all the time.

fills.explanation: The spiritual reading says the natural mind "relates" to the Dragon; in Kephalaia register, "this earth is likened to it" expresses the correspondence between the body/natural mind and the Dragon allegory.
The spiritual reading says "the selfhood ruling through the external person"; in natural-plane Kephalaia register, "a corporeal Dragon in the body" locates the Dragon within the physical person.
The spiritual reading says "I will open this to your understanding"; in Kephalaia style, "I will instruct you about this" introduces the doctrinal explanation that follows.

The spiritual reading says "governing principle"; in ¶7 the Dragon is explicitly called "the thought of the body," confirming that "doctrine and thought" together constitute the Dragon's governing principle.

The spiritual reading says "of the natural and unregenerate person"; Kephalaia style commonly pairs "flesh" and "body" (as σάρξ and σῶμα), so "of the flesh and of the body" captures both the natural and unregenerate aspects.

Following the established pattern of "the two of sight," "the two of sound," "the two of scent," the tongue naturally takes the descriptor "of taste," and the spiritual reading confirms this as "the faculty of discriminating appetite."

The spiritual reading says "and those belonging to the lower, exterior natural part"; the gap introduces the seven lower faculties as a counterpart to the seven upper ones, requiring a transitional phrase leading into "below."
In the Manichaean body-schema, the paired organs of the torso/lower body begin with the hands (grasping/action), corresponding to the volitional faculties in the spiritual reading.

Following the hands, the feet are the second natural pair of the lower body in Manichaean anthropology, representing movement/direction and corresponding to volitional faculties in the spiritual reading.

The spiritual reading says "corresponding to the seven governing falsities that operate from above"; "over against" is the standard Kephalaia expression for correspondence between upper and lower counterparts.

fills.explanation: The editor's reconstruction aligns precisely with the spiritual reading: "reveal its likeness" = "manifest its character," "its observation" = "its vigilance," "above and below" = "rational and natural faculties," "wages war" = "wages spiritual combat."

fills.fill: that one, he is called a slayer of the Dragon
fills.explanation: The spiritual reading says "that person is called a regenerate being"; in the natural-plane allegory of this chapter, one who conquers the Dragon of the selfhood is called a Dragon-slayer, consistent with the Zoroastrian-Iranian heroic tradition underlying the Kephalaia's imagery.

fills.fill: all that it wills, pursuing its lust and its des
fills.explanation: The spiritual reading says "according to its ruling love and its insatiable appetite"; in Kephalaia register, the Dragon acts through the five dens doing "all that it wills" (ruling love) and pursuing "its lust and its desire" (insatiable appetite).
